prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye. Round 1 did not weaken the core of the case and strengthened two parts of it. First, four members (Johansson, Lindroth, Pearce and I) now place it first, and each of the other four names it as a fall-back, so it is the configuration least likely to be an unwelcome outcome for anyone. I do not treat that count as evidence in itself, but it came from members with different tastes who checked the same physical facts. Second, the experimental record is the kind I trust most: the magic-wavelength condition removes the dominant systematic for thousands of atoms interrogated at once, and 1e-18 fractional uncertainty has been compared across JILA/NIST, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE and PTB with the blackbody, lattice-shift and collisional corrections independently understood. What it opens is already physics: the gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and on ultralight dark-matter couplings, and relativistic geodesy. Credit is as clean as this shortlist offers: Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for taking it to record accuracy and stability. For the citation I propose wording around the lattice clock and its realisation at 1e-18, with no reference to the frequency comb and no reference to the redefinition of the second, which is a metrological decision and not a physics discovery. This also answers the chair's question on the second.
statement.case_against: The serious reservation is the one Olsson, Eriksson, Mehlig and Danielsson press: after the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, a lattice-clock award can read as a refinement of an honoured line, and Ye's role risks looking like better execution of Katori's idea. I have weighed that and still think the lattice is a distinct conceptual step; the many-atom regime is separate from single-ion statistics and from counting optical cycles. But I accept that it is a judgment, and that a member who weights new matter or a new window on nature over a new measurement regime will reasonably prefer B019 or B032. Credit is also not perfectly tidy. Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB and SYRTE groups made decisive demonstrations, and I cannot settle priority from memory. The possible later thorium-clock candidacy for Ye is a strategic complication, but a prize should not be withheld for a hypothetical later award.

responses.point: Olsson asks what Ye's clocks add that is original rather than merely superior, and worries that the pattern credits the most beautiful execution and not the original experiment.
responses.response: I will answer concretely. Katori's contribution is the idea and the first demonstration, and I would not blur that. What Ye's group added was not only a lower number. The systematic budget at 1e-18 required new understanding: the blackbody shift, higher-order light shifts, tunnelling and collisional shifts in the lattice, and a clock laser with coherence long enough to use the atoms' coherence time. The spin-polarised fermionic Sr clock with its collisional control and the cavity-stabilised laser were what made the stability and the systematic measurements credible. Those are things that a different group could not simply have executed from Katori's paper. That is why I would word Ye's part as realisation at record accuracy and stability and not as comb work. It is also why I think the two-name split is not only a courtesy. I accept that this answer does not remove the priority claims of Lemonde, Ludlow and Takamoto, and I would not claim it does. I would like to hear whether you now see the pair as a defensible mature outcome, since you already call B042 your first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B019 as a revelation of new matter, calls lattice clocks an extraordinary refinement of a capability earlier prizes opened, and asks whether Ye's comb and cavity-stabilisation work is separable from 2005.
responses.response: On your direct question: yes, I think it is separable. The comb counts optical cycles; it is a link between optical and microwave frequencies and was recognised as such. The lattice clock is a different object, an ensemble of trapped atoms whose transition is interrogated with the laser and whose systematics are controlled at the 1e-18 level. Ye used a comb and a stabilised cavity, just as every optical clock does, but the citation need not mention either, and I would insist that it does not. On discovery versus refinement, I take your point that B019 revealed new matter and that this is the stronger story in kind. My reservation about waiting remains concrete: the pairing mechanism and the nature of several correlated states are unresolved, Yuan Cao and others are outside the three names, and the Lopes dos Santos earlier twist-angle theory is a further question. You say yourself that B042 is the better-settled discovery and that you would support it. I find that candid and it matters to me. If the committee cannot settle the B019 names, I would not regard B019 as a worse outcome than B042 in scientific terms, only as one I cannot yet vouch for as I can for the clock.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, now ranks B042 first, keeps B032 as his main alternative as a more direct new observational window, and notes the possible later thorium-clock candidacy for Ye.
responses.response: I agree with the maturity ordering you give and with the thorium point, which I raised myself; I would not let a hypothetical later award decide this one. On B032, I take the new-window argument seriously and that is why I now list it as an alternative. My remaining reservations are the ones you named: the diffuse flux is secure but individual sources are at 3-4 sigma, and the pioneer credit (AMANDA, Baikal, DUMAND, ANTARES) makes the pair Halzen and Spiering harder to defend than Katori and Ye. The chair asked whether the expert reports establish Spiering's role as decisive; I cannot answer that from the material I am allowed to see, and I would not support B032 unless that is settled.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B042 but asks whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second, and whether Ye alone or other JILA and NIST contributors is the right second name.
responses.response: I would not wait for the redefinition. It is decided by a metrological body on its own schedule, which is a different kind of decision from our judgment on whether a discovery or invention is prize-worthy, and tying our timing to it would let that schedule govern the Nobel prize. The performance and its independent reproduction exist today. On the second name, I looked at what each candidate would add. Adding Lemonde or Takamoto would mean a third name for an early demonstration, while Ye's group is the one that carried the full performance programme and cross-comparisons. I think Katori and Ye is the right pair, with the other names appearing in the scientific background. I will not claim certainty from memory on first-demonstration priority, and if the committee's outside evaluations show an earlier claim, I would reconsider.

responses.point: Danielsson places a new window on nature above another factor of ten in precision, prefers B032, but would not resist B042 if the committee prefers the metrology line.
responses.response: I do not think 1e-18 is only another factor of ten. Below roughly 1e-17 the clock becomes a gravitational and field sensor: an optical lattice clock resolves the redshift over a millimetre, and clock networks are used to search for dark matter and for variation of constants. That is a new way of observing nature, and in my experience measurement capability is what limits knowledge. I accept that an astronomical window like IceCube is the more obvious discovery in the sense you use. I would say that the diffuse flux alone does not yet give a prize citation as secure as the clock, because individual sources are not established, but I respect that you hold it with more conviction than I do and I would not oppose B032 on principle.

uncertainties: Priority among the first lattice-clock demonstrations (Katori, Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Hinkley, Bloom); I rely on memory and would reconsider the pair if outside evaluations show an earlier decisive claim.
Whether the committee reads lattice clocks as meeting the will as a discovery or invention given the 2005 and 2012 prizes; this is a judgment on which I may be too close to the measurement community.

For B019, whether the pairing mechanism will clarify enough in the next few years to change the case, and whether Yuan Cao and the Lopes dos Santos theory can be handled in citation wording; I cannot settle this from the supplied record.
For B032 I changed my listed alternative from B050 to B032 because B050 still has an unresolved three-person allocation, but I cannot verify Spiering's role relative to other pioneers.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. During my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye is at JILA in the same community. I have no collaboration, supervision, funding or institutional tie to Katori or Ye that I know of, and I do not regard this as recusal-level; I note it so the committee can judge. I have a Lund and WACQT connection through quantum technology, but no tie to any other credited name on the shortlist. I will keep my argument on the scientific record and not on my familiarity with the metrology community.
